clue.text: A musical monologue hardly true — and addressed to Celia

parts.note: rap is a spoken-word musical form, one voice delivering a monologue over a beat

indicators.note: something hardly true is not quite right, so its letters are put slightly out of order

explanation.surface: Someone describes a sung soliloquy as barely truthful, yet dedicated to a woman named Celia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hardly' rearranges TRUE into TURE. Thomas Carew's love poem A Rapture is addressed to Celia, as several Cavalier poems were.
explanation.definitionFit: Carew's erotic poem carrying that title speaks throughout to his mistress Celia, so the work is identified by its addressee.

clue.text: Mayne presented one in May (1,7)

parts.note: William Mayne's 1955 children's novel about a cathedral choir school is titled after a bee colony appearing in that month

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'a swarm in May is worth a load of hay' gives Mayne's title; the clue reads as if Mayne presented a single item in spring.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of William Mayne's novel names one bee colony appearing in May, and the clue's 'one in May' points straight to it.

clue.text: Not quite an aspect of Osborne's gentility

definitions.meaning: not quite means nearly, just short of
John Osborne's second volume of autobiography is titled ... a Gentleman, so this word is the qualifier on his gentility

explanation.surface: A remark that something is only partly true of the playwright John Osborne's refinement.
explanation.definitionFit: Not quite is the everyday synonym of nearly; the second sense comes from the title of Osborne's memoir, which hedges his claim to be a gentleman.

clue.text: Sad actor not good at reading

indicators.note: letters that are not good are in poor order, signalling that the words before them are rearranged

explanation.surface: A gloomy performer who is poor at reading his script aloud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not good' rearranges the nine letters of AT READING.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer specialising in tragic roles plays the sad parts, hence a sad actor.

clue.text: New Zealander's view of progressive Cumbrian

definitions.text: New Zealander's view of progressive Cumbrian

parts.words: New Zealander's view of progressive Cumbrian
parts.note: Hugh Walpole, born in Auckland, wrote a novel about a wild Cumberland squire that opens a family saga progressing through generations

explanation.walkthrough: Walpole was born in New Zealand; his Herries Chronicle begins with this novel set in Cumberland (Cumbria, in northwest England) and moves forward through the family's history.
explanation.definitionFit: The title names Walpole's Cumbrian hero Francis Herries, so the novel is a New Zealand-born author's portrait of a Cumbrian.

clue.text: Trap associated with arachnid (or moth?)

parts.note: a spider spins a silken snare, and in A Midsummer Night's Dream a fairy bearing that snare's name attends Titania alongside one called Moth

explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed 'or moth?' points to Shakespeare's fairies Peaseblossom, Moth, Mustardseed and the one named after the spider's trap.
explanation.definitionFit: A spider's dusty web is a trap tied to an arachnid, and Shakespeare gave the same name to a fairy who serves beside Moth.

clue.text: His rage was for life, his appointment with Death

definitions.text: His rage was for life, his appointment with Death

parts.words: His rage was for life, his appointment with Death
parts.note: the American novelist John wrote A Rage to Live and Appointment in Samarra, the latter titled from the fable of meeting Death

explanation.walkthrough: Appointment in Samarra takes its title from the old tale in which a servant flees Death only to meet him in Samarra.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue strings together two of John's novel titles, A Rage to Live and Appointment in Samarra, identifying the American author.

clue.text: Brendan Behan's hostage

parts.note: in Behan's play The Hostage the captive held in a Dublin lodging house is a young English soldier, Leslie

explanation.definitionFit: The English soldier Leslie, held by the IRA in Behan's play The Hostage, bears this surname.

clue.text: Poet getting a tan

definitions.meaning: Robert or Elizabeth Barrett, the Victorian poets

explanation.surface: A versifier heads off to sunbathe.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Browning is a celebrated Victorian poet, and turning brown in the sun is the literal sense of getting a tan.

clue.text: His choir boys practised in MacArthur Park

definitions.text: His choir boys practised in MacArthur Park

parts.words: His choir boys practised in MacArthur Park
parts.note: the policeman-novelist's The Choirboys follows Los Angeles cops whose drunken 'choir practice' sessions take place in that park

explanation.walkthrough: In Joseph Wambaugh's The Choirboys, 'choir practice' is the officers' name for their after-shift binges in MacArthur Park, Los Angeles.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph, the former LAPD officer turned novelist, wrote The Choirboys, whose cops hold their choir practice in MacArthur Park.

clue.text: He would not pass judgment on Paul and still avoids responsibility

definitions.text: He would not pass judgment on Paul
definitions.meaning: in Acts 18 the Roman proconsul of Achaia dismissed the case brought against Paul, caring for none of those things
the proconsul's name became a byword for an official who shirks duty or stays indifferent

explanation.surface: The Roman governor who declined to try Paul is still described as dodging his duty.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical proconsul's indifference made his name a common noun for anyone careless of matters outside their concern.

clue.text: Ridicule beach girls from Runyon

parts.note: to guy someone is to mock or ridicule them
sand is the stuff of a beach
dolls is slang for attractive girls

explanation.surface: Someone mocks the girls on the beach, in the style of Damon Runyon.
explanation.walkthrough: Damon Runyon's Broadway stories gave rise to the musical; its title is literally Runyon slang for men and women.
explanation.definitionFit: The musical was drawn from Damon Runyon's stories of Broadway gamblers, so it comes from Runyon.

clue.text: Amiable Cotswold drinking companion

parts.note: Laurie Lee's memoir of a Gloucestershire village is titled Cider with her, the girl he shares the drink with

explanation.walkthrough: Laurie Lee's Cider with Rosie recalls a childhood in Slad, in the Cotswolds hills of Gloucestershire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: In Laurie Lee's memoir title the narrator shares cider with this girl, his friendly Cotswold drinking partner.

clue.text: 23 of Blackwood had one

parts.note: Algernon Blackwood wrote The ... of Uncle Paul, so the relative at 23 in that title received schooling

explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to 23-across; Blackwood's 1909 novel title tells what that relative, Paul, had.
explanation.definitionFit: Blackwood's novel title says Paul, the relative of 23, received schooling of this kind.

clue.text: Thracian flower did not overawe Xerxes (nor Mrs Verity, oddly enough)

definitions.text: Thracian flower did not overawe Xerxes

indicators.note: something done oddly is done in a strange way, here signalling the preceding letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: An ancient Greek waterway fails to impress the Persian king, and a Mrs Verity is equally unmoved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly enough' rearranges NOR MRS VERITY. 'Flower' is a crossword river, something that flows; Herodotus tells how Xerxes crossed the Strymon in Thrace on his march into Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: The Strymon is a river of ancient Thrace that Xerxes bridged on his invasion, a Thracian flowing thing he was not deterred by.

clue.text: Use 13 again

parts.note: putting the schooling of 13-across to work a second time means teaching someone anew

explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference is to 13-across; a dropped digit in the printed clue gives '3'.
explanation.definitionFit: To teach again, or train someone in new ways, is applying instruction a second time.

clue.text: Early presenter of The Gladiators

parts.note: Arthur, the Hungarian-born author, published a novel about Spartacus's revolt titled The Gladiators in 1939, long before the TV show of that name

explanation.walkthrough: 'Presenter' suggests a host of the British TV game show Gladiators; it means the author who first presented the story in 1939.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Koestler's first novel, The Gladiators, retold the Spartacus revolt decades before the television show of the same name.

clue.text: Lucetta thought him a knight well spoken, neat and fine

definitions.text: Lucetta thought him a knight well spoken, neat and fine

parts.words: Lucetta thought him a knight well spoken, neat and fine
parts.note: in The Two Gentlemen of Verona the maid Lucetta describes Julia's suitor Sir ... as 'a knight well-spoken, neat and fine'

explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Lucetta gives exactly these words about Sir Eglamour when Julia asks her opinion of her suitors.

clue.text: There is no need to attack the monkey when the is present" (Aneurin Bevan)

definitions.text: There is no need to attack the monkey when the is present" (Aneurin Bevan)

parts.words: There is no need to attack the monkey when the is present" (Aneurin Bevan)
parts.note: Bevan's jibe completes with the street musician whose monkey merely collects coins, meaning the boss who really controls things

explanation.walkthrough: The gap in Bevan's quotation is the street musician who turns a barrel organ while his monkey begs; the phrase means the person in charge.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrel-organ player is the monkey's master, and Bevan used him to mean the real power behind a subordinate.

clue.text: What tidings send our? I prithee, speak (Henry VI, Part I)

definitions.text: What tidings send our? I prithee, speak (Henry VI, Part I)

parts.words: What tidings send our? I prithee, speak (Henry VI, Part I)
parts.note: the missing word in Shakespeare's line is the spies sent ahead to bring back news

explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's line asks what news the advance spies send, so the gap is filled by those reconnaissance men.

clue.text: Outward appearance as presented by Dickensian arriviste?

definitions.meaning: a thin surface layer or show hiding what lies beneath
the Veneerings in Our Mutual Friend are newly rich social climbers whose very name advertises a thin shiny coating

explanation.surface: The image projected by one of Dickens's upstart social climbers.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin decorative layer over cheaper wood gives the sense of a superficial outward show.

clue.text: Borders are invaded by Dickensian nasty

definitions.meaning: garden flower beds get overrun by small unwanted plants
Grandfather ... is the grasping moneylender in Bleak House

explanation.surface: Garden beds overrun by a horrid character out of Dickens.
explanation.definitionFit: Garden borders are overrun by little unwanted plants, and the same name belongs to the grasping family in Bleak House.

clue.text: Boy at home producing language of Romance

parts.note: a lad is a boy
in means at home

explanation.surface: A boy who stays indoors writes a love story.
explanation.definitionFit: Ladin is a Romance tongue spoken in the Dolomite valleys of northern Italy, descended from Latin.

clue.text: Horace seen as relative by Mrs Hall

definitions.text: Horace seen as relative by Mrs Hall

parts.words: Horace seen as relative by Mrs Hall
parts.note: Mrs S. C. Hall published an 1837 novel about an eccentric bachelor named Horace, titled for his family role toward his niece

explanation.walkthrough: Anna Maria Hall, who wrote as Mrs S. C. Hall, made her eccentric Horace a family elder protecting his niece Mary.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Hall's novel casts Horace as the brother of a parent, the kinsman watching over his niece.

clue.text: Dorothy Dunnett's hero's yacht's mistaken insurers?

indicators.note: a name got wrong has its letters in the wrong order

parts.note: Johnson Johnson, the portrait-painter sleuth of Dorothy Dunnett's thrillers, sails a yacht called Dolly

explanation.surface: The boat belonging to a thriller writer's hero has been wrongly identified as belonging to an insurance firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mistaken' rearranges DOLLYS. The London insurance market, Lloyd's, is a body of underwriters, hence the question mark on 'insurers'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lloyd's of London is the famous insurance market, its members underwriting risks, especially shipping, which suits a yacht.

clue.text: Delight given by Waugh's work

definitions.meaning: Alec Waugh published a 1921 book with this title

explanation.surface: The enjoyment gained from reading a Waugh book.
explanation.definitionFit: Delight and gratification are near synonyms, and Alec Waugh used the word as a book title.

clue.text: Second performances concerning scores

parts.note: re means concerning or about
runs are what a batsman scores in cricket

explanation.surface: Repeat shows getting good marks from critics.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the score is counted in runs.
explanation.definitionFit: Repeated broadcasts or stagings of a show are its second and later performances.

clue.text: He values one like Modestine, perhaps, with an alternative

parts.note: Modestine is the donkey in Stevenson's Travels with a Donkey in the Cevennes, a she-ass, playfully a female ass with the -ess ending as in lioness
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: A man who weighs up Stevenson's donkey, or something else instead.
explanation.walkthrough: Modestine was a female donkey, so the setter coins a feminine of 'ass' on the pattern of lioness.
explanation.definitionFit: A valuer appraises property, judging its worth, so he values things for a living.
